question: SQ-LIP-000001
text: Is lipedema a distinct disease, separate from obesity and lymphedema?
minor_problems: [minor] set: The core claim in P1 rests on consensus and expert opinion. E2 and E12 have null quotes, so their findings cannot be checked against text. E34, E10 and E27 qualify the picture (frequent coexistence, almost exclusively in obese women, lymphedema rising with BMI) but only partly reach P1's wording.

[minor] set: P5 and P7 sit in tension with E26 (frequent lymphatic abnormalities in lipedema, unrelated to BMI), which is filed only as 'refines' under P5. A caveat on the imaging-based distinction should carry through to P1.
[minor] set: P8 (metabolic comorbidity) and P9 (blood count) are tangential to the question and are single-study findings. They add little to the answer on distinctness and could be context-only.

[minor] set: E10 is labelled supporting in P1 although its quote concerns occurrence in obese women. E1's finding text mentions BMI of limited value, which is not in the quote, so that detail is unverifiable.

[minor] P1: not fully supported; overgeneralized; two ideas; stance errors ['E10'] — suggested: Lipedema is widely regarded as a clinical entity distinct from obesity and lymphedema, based mainly on expert opinion and clinical features, though overlap and coexistence occur. (Support is almost entirely consensus, expert opinion and narrative reviews (E2 and E12 have no quote and cannot be checked; E2 is labelled expert_opinion yet summarised as a narrative review). Distinctness from obesity and from lymphedema rests on different evidence. E10 says lipedema occurs almost exclusively in obese women, which is context, not support for distinctness. Data-based support sits in P4 and P5, and E34 and E26 qualify the categorical wording.)

[minor] P3: misplaced ['E5'] — suggested: Foot sparing, negative Stemmer sign, bilateral symmetry, easy bruising and painful fat are reported to help distinguish early lipedema from lymphedema clinically. (E12 itself says Stemmer becomes positive with lipolymphedema, and E26 found lymphatic involvement unrelated to Stemmer, so the signs apply mainly to early or pure lipedema. The CT sensitivity and specificity in E5 belong with imaging (P5), not clinical signs. E22 is only 9 patients.)

[minor] P4: not fully supported; overgeneralized; two ideas; misplaced ['E13'] — suggested: Lipedema adipose tissue is reported to show histological and molecular features that differ from BMI-matched controls, and some that differ from lymphedema. (The BMI-matched comparator evidence is E16 and E20 (small samples). The lymphedema comparator evidence is only E17 and E15. E13 is a commentary on normal-BMI patients with no stated comparator, and E15 and E18 are reviews with no stated obesity comparator, so they do not show differences from tissue of similar body mass. The statement bundles two comparisons.)

[minor] P5: not fully supported; overgeneralized; misplaced ['E3'] — suggested: Lymphatic imaging in lipedema often shows patterns that differ from lymphedema, although lymphatic abnormalities are also frequent in lipedema and do not exclude it. (E3 compares pure lipedema with lipolymphedema, not lymphedema, and fits coexistence better. E24 and E29 are small series. E26 (47% abnormal lymphoscintigraphy) shows that imaging does not cleanly separate the two, which the flat wording hides.)

items.title: Brazilian Consensus Statement on Lipedema using the Delphi methodology
items.quote: distribuição desproporcional de TAS e ausência de relação causal com obesidade
items.note: Brazilian Delphi consensus (expert agreement, not primary evidence)
old_statements: Lipedema is a distinct clinical entity separate from obesity and lymphedema, although all three can coexist.

Lipedema is defined by a disproportionate, symmetrical accumulation of subcutaneous adipose tissue in the limbs relative to the trunk that is characteristically resistant to conventional weight-loss methods (diet and exercise), distinguishing it from common obesity.
In the Brazilian Delphi consensus, experts agreed that lipedema and obesity do not have a causal relationship and that BMI is of limited value in differentiating lipedema from obesity.

Clinical signs that help diagnose lipedema and distinguish it from lymphedema include a usually negative Kaposi-Stemmer sign, the cuff sign with foot sparing, fat painful on palpation, easy bruising, and minimal pitting edema (Stemmer becomes positive only when secondary lymphedema/lipolymphedema develops).
Patients with lipedema frequently report swelling and a sensation of heaviness in the affected limbs.

items.title: Lipedema and obesity: biological interactions, diagnostic challenges, and staged interdisciplinary management
items.quote: Although often approached as differential diagnoses, they frequently coexist and may aggravate one another.
items.note: The review emphasizes overlap and bidirectional interaction between lipedema and obesity (and lymphatic dysfunction) rather than affirming lipedema as a cleanly separate entity; it qualifies the distinctness by stressing coexistence and sha
old_statements: This narrative review argues that lipedema and obesity, though often treated as mutually exclusive differential diagnoses, frequently coexist and interact via a bidirectional loop between adiposity and lymphatic function, supporting a staged interdisciplinary approach rather than treatment as mutually exclusive entities.

propositions.statement: Lipedema is a clinical entity distinct from obesity and lymphedema, although the three conditions can coexist.
propositions.rationale: Consensus statements and reviews (low-grade, mostly expert opinion) consistently frame lipedema as a separate entity; E8 and E11 only frame differential diagnosis (context) and E31 adds a patient-reported distinction.

evidence.finding: Brazilian Delphi consensus (113 experts) agreed on disproportionate subcutaneous fat distribution and absence of a causal relationship with obesity; BMI judged of limited value to separate lipedema from obesity.
Narrative review describing lipedema as a distinct clinical entity separate from obesity and lymphedema, while noting the three can coexist.
Systematic review of hormonal mechanisms concluded findings support reclassifying lipedema as a hormonally influenced disorder distinct from obesity.
Narrative review stated lipedema appears to be a clinical entity related to genetic factors and fat distribution, distinct from lymphedema and obesity, while noting scarce high-quality trials.
Narrative review stated diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation of pain, palpation and fat distribution with exclusion of lymphedema and simple obesity; no original comparative data.
Review stated lipohyperplasia dolorosa and lymphedema are completely different disease entities, both classified under lymphology, with lipedema commonly confused with obesity.

Review described lipedema as an adipose tissue disorder, occurring almost exclusively in obese women, frequently misdiagnosed as primary lymphedema, distinguished by foot sparing and poor response to weight loss.
Review listed obesity, lipohypertrophy and primary and secondary lymphedema as the main differential diagnoses of lipedema.
Comparative analysis of two cases concluded lipedema and lymphedema differ in epidemiology, histopathology, clinical signs, imaging and treatment, and are often confused.
In 151 women, lipoedema (90) had higher LYMQOL symptom, appearance and mood burden and worse LSIDS-L neurological scores than bilateral leg lymphoedema (61), despite similar symptoms.

propositions.statement: Lipedema fat in the affected limbs is reported to resist diet, exercise and bariatric weight loss, unlike common obesity.
propositions.rationale: Several reviews cite resistance of limb fat to weight-loss interventions as a central clinical difference from obesity.

evidence.finding: Narrative review stated lipedema of the legs does not respond to restrictive diet, the main clinical distinction from simple obesity.
Review described lipedema fat as resistant to diet and exercise, with weight lost in unaffected areas and bariatric surgery ineffective for affected limbs.
Practical guide stated diet and exercise do not reduce affected extremities and bariatric surgery does not make lipedema disappear, separating it from adiposity.

propositions.statement: Foot sparing, a negative Stemmer sign, bilateral symmetry, easy bruising and painful fat help distinguish lipedema from lymphedema clinically.
propositions.rationale: Clinical series and reviews describe a consistent set of bedside signs separating lipedema from lymphedema.

evidence.finding: Case report with comparative table: usually negative Kaposi-Stemmer sign, cuff sign with foot sparing, painful fat, easy bruising and minimal pitting; Stemmer turns positive when lipolymphedema develops.

Literature review: lipoedema differs from lymphoedema by negative Stemmer sign, no foot involvement, spontaneous pain and bruising, bilateral symmetry, plus distinct histopathology; proposes a diagnostic algorithm.
Among 250 lower extremity lymphedema referrals, 9 lipedema patients showed bilateral symmetric swelling sparing the feet, absent Stemmer sign and fat pads anterior to the lateral malleoli.
Systematic review: foot sparing (cuff sign) and negative Stemmer sign are key differentials from lymphedema; non-contrast CT reported sensitivity 95% and specificity 100% for lipedema.

propositions.statement: Lipedema adipose tissue is reported to show histological and molecular features that differ from control tissue of similar body mass and from lymphedema.
propositions.rationale: Small tissue studies, a commentary and reviews report distinct adipocyte, inflammatory, vascular and gene expression profiles versus BMI-matched (not obese) controls, lipohypertrophy and lymphedema.

evidence.finding: Versus BMI-matched controls, lipedema tissue showed adipocyte hypertrophy, intercellular fibrosis, epidermal thickening, aberrant lipid metabolism and a distinct adipogenesis gene expression profile (small sample).
Comparing lipedema, lipohypertrophy and secondary lymphedema, VEGF-R3 was increased only in lymphedema (3.2-fold vs 1.0 in lipedema), indicating distinct histological and molecular profiles.

Biopsies from 11 lipedema vs 10 BMI-matched healthy controls: CD45+ leukocytes 40.7 vs 20 per field, CD68+ macrophages increased with M2 polarisation, serum VEGF-C elevated, no lymphatic morphology changes.

Commentary on histopathology in normal-BMI early-stage lipedema: macrophage infiltration only in affected areas, endothelial and pericyte hyperproliferation and barrier degeneration, indicating pathology independent of obesity.

Review: lipedema lacks the T-cell signature of lymphedema, shows fibrotic extracellular matrix and elevated VEGF-C without altered lymphatic architecture; the two diverge in time course, regulators and genetics.
Review: exosome, cytokine, lipidomic and metabolomic profiling suggest lipedema is distinct from obesity and lymphedema, with fat cell hyperproliferation, fibrosis and inflammation.

propositions.statement: Lymphatic imaging shows patterns in lipedema that differ from lymphedema.
propositions.rationale: MR, fluorescence and lymphoscintigraphic studies report distinguishing lymphatic features (only E14 adds BMI-matched controls), though lymphatic abnormalities also occur in lipedema (E26).

evidence.finding: Non-contrast MR lymphography: fat homogeneous without edema in pure lipedema, whereas all lipolymphedema extremities showed epifascial high-signal areas on 3D-TSE (p<.001).

3T MR lymphangiography showed distinct subcutaneous hyperintensity patterns separating lipedema, lipedema with lymphedema and cancer-related lymphedema from BMI-matched controls; dilated vascular pattern more frequent in cancer lymphedema (OR 12.27).
Near-infrared fluorescence imaging of 20 stage I-II lipedema patients: dilated lymphatics, increased propulsion (1.4 vs 0.9 events/min) and no dermal backflow in any leg, in contrast to lymphedema.
Lymphoscintigraphy in 15 lipedema vs 15 primary lymphedema: inguinal nodes absent in 14/15 lymphedema vs 1/15 lipedema (p<0.001); colloid half-life 230 vs 121 min; weight loss spares limb fat.
In 83 women with lipedema, lymphoscintigraphy showed lymphatic alterations in 47% (mostly low grade), unrelated to stage or BMI; abnormal findings do not exclude lipedema.

propositions.statement: Lipedema may coexist with obesity and with lymphedema in the same patient.
propositions.rationale: A narrative review and case reports document overlap, qualifying a clean separation; whether one condition aggravates the other is not shown here, and E1 states no causal relation with obesity.

evidence.finding: Narrative review: although approached as differential diagnoses, lipedema and obesity frequently coexist and may aggravate one another through a loop between adiposity and lymphatic function.
Woman with lipedema and grade I lymphedema: lymph drainage and compression reduced leg volume by 10.6% and 6.8% in three days while lipedema fat accumulation persisted.

Male with lipedema and post-surgical lymphedema progressed from subclinical to clinical systemic lymphedema over three years by bioimpedance; authors cite lymphedema in half of lipedema with BMI over 30.

propositions.statement: Lymphedema in people with lipedema is reported to be more frequent at higher body mass index.
propositions.rationale: A single cross-sectional study links lymphedema frequency to BMI within lipedema, a distinct idea from mere coexistence (P6), so it is hedged.

evidence.finding: In 258 women with lipedema, clinical lymphedema rose from 6.1% (BMI<30) to 51.6% (30-40) and 77.8% (40-50), p=0.0001; edema also occurred at normal weight.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Lymphedema in women with lipedema appears more frequent with higher body mass.

propositions.statement: Limited evidence suggests lipedema may be accompanied by lower rates of metabolic comorbidity than in women of similar age in the general population.
propositions.rationale: A single chart review compared with age-matched general-population women, not with obese women, so selection bias is likely and wording is hedged.

evidence.finding: In 46 women with lipedema (mean BMI 35.3), diabetes 2% vs about 10% in age-matched NHANES women, dyslipidemia 11.7% vs 33.5%, hypertension 13% vs 32.4%; fat not reduced by lifestyle change.

propositions.statement: Routine blood count parameters may not distinguish women with lipedema from controls.
propositions.rationale: A null blood-based finding is a separate axis from tissue histology, so it gets its own hedged proposition.

evidence.finding: In 45 women with lipedema vs 40 age-matched (not BMI-matched) controls, no complete blood count parameter differed significantly after multiple-comparison correction; PDW and MPV only numerically higher.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Lipedema is widely regarded as a clinical entity distinct from obesity and lymphedema, based mainly on expert opinion and clinical features, though overlap and coexistence occur.
verdicts.note: Support is almost entirely consensus, expert opinion and narrative reviews (E2 and E12 have no quote and cannot be checked; E2 is labelled expert_opinion yet summarised as a narrative review). Distinctness from obesity and from lymphedema rests on different evidence. E10 says lipedema occurs almost exclusively in obese women, which is context, not support for distinctness. Data-based support sits in P4 and P5, and E34 and E26 qualify the categorical wording.
Three narrative or practical reviews with no primary data, but the wording is 'is reported', which matches the evidence.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Foot sparing, negative Stemmer sign, bilateral symmetry, easy bruising and painful fat are reported to help distinguish early lipedema from lymphedema clinically.
verdicts.note: E12 itself says Stemmer becomes positive with lipolymphedema, and E26 found lymphatic involvement unrelated to Stemmer, so the signs apply mainly to early or pure lipedema. The CT sensitivity and specificity in E5 belong with imaging (P5), not clinical signs. E22 is only 9 patients.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Lipedema adipose tissue is reported to show histological and molecular features that differ from BMI-matched controls, and some that differ from lymphedema.
verdicts.note: The BMI-matched comparator evidence is E16 and E20 (small samples). The lymphedema comparator evidence is only E17 and E15. E13 is a commentary on normal-BMI patients with no stated comparator, and E15 and E18 are reviews with no stated obesity comparator, so they do not show differences from tissue of similar body mass. The statement bundles two comparisons.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Lymphatic imaging in lipedema often shows patterns that differ from lymphedema, although lymphatic abnormalities are also frequent in lipedema and do not exclude it.
verdicts.note: E3 compares pure lipedema with lipolymphedema, not lymphedema, and fits coexistence better. E24 and E29 are small series. E26 (47% abnormal lymphoscintigraphy) shows that imaging does not cleanly separate the two, which the flat wording hides.
Hedged with 'may'. Case reports plus a narrative review are adequate for a coexistence claim. E27 also supports it and is placed under P7.

A single cross-sectional study, but the wording 'appears' is suitably hedged. Mild tension with E26, where lymphoscintigraphic involvement was unrelated to BMI; the outcomes differ, so it is not a direct contradiction.

Hedged and the comparator (general population, not obese women) is stated correctly. It is tangential to the question of whether lipedema is a distinct disease, and does not itself separate lipedema from obesity.
One exploratory study with a non-BMI-matched comparator, and the wording is 'may not'. Marginal relevance to distinctness.

set_issues.issue: The core claim in P1 rests on consensus and expert opinion. E2 and E12 have null quotes, so their findings cannot be checked against text. E34, E10 and E27 qualify the picture (frequent coexistence, almost exclusively in obese women, lymphedema rising with BMI) but only partly reach P1's wording.

P5 and P7 sit in tension with E26 (frequent lymphatic abnormalities in lipedema, unrelated to BMI), which is filed only as 'refines' under P5. A caveat on the imaging-based distinction should carry through to P1.
P8 (metabolic comorbidity) and P9 (blood count) are tangential to the question and are single-study findings. They add little to the answer on distinctness and could be context-only.
E10 is labelled supporting in P1 although its quote concerns occurrence in obese women. E1's finding text mentions BMI of limited value, which is not in the quote, so that detail is unverifiable.
